message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, please don't run it. The line is wrong, and it could cause harm.

## What's wrong with it
- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.** They have no effect on flu and won't get anyone back to work sooner. Doctors generally won't tell you otherwise, and official health guidance in the UK and elsewhere advises against using antibiotics for flu.
- **Taking antibiotics unnecessarily has real downsides.** They can cause side effects such as nausea, diarrhoea and allergic reactions, and overuse drives antibiotic resistance, which makes them less effective when people genuinely need them.
- **Encouraging staff to ask for them puts pressure on GPs** to prescribe something that won't help.

## Why his GP may have prescribed them
Flu sometimes leads to a secondary *bacterial* infection, such as a chest infection or sinusitis, and antibiotics are appropriate for those. His GP may have been treating a complication, or an illness that wasn't flu. That doesn't mean antibiotics treat flu itself.

There *are* antiviral medicines for flu. They're usually reserved for people at higher risk of complications and work best when started early. That decision belongs to a doctor, not to a newsletter tip.

## Suggested replacement line
> **Flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. The best protection is the annual flu jab. If you do catch flu, rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids and stay off work until you feel better, so you don't pass it on. Call your GP or a pharmacist if your symptoms are severe, you're in a higher-risk group, or you're not improving after a week.**

If your company offers flu jabs or vouchers, this is a good place to mention them.

## Raising it with him
It may help to frame the change as tightening up the advice rather than correcting him. You could say you checked it against NHS guidance, which separates flu from the bacterial infections that sometimes follow it. His instinct to help staff recover faster is a good one; it just needs pointing at the advice that actually works.
